1527.dq: In words of two, three, or four syllables, the heavy syllable closest to the end of the word, not counting the last syllable, probably took the stress. (Skjaervo 2016: 18); Kent: 'the presence of enclitic words shows that there was an accent.'
1527.dloc: Kent 1950 sec. 59(i), p. 25 (chapter Phonology); Skjaervo 2016 p. 18
1527.heavy: (conjectural only, Skjaervo 2016) a syllable with a long vowel or a diphthong or a short vowel followed by more than one consonant
1527.prule: No direct evidence: the OP cuneiform script does not mark accent; Kent states position and nature of the word accent are unknown, only its existence being inferable from enclitics. Skjaervo 2016 p. 18 adds a comparative conjecture, not an attested fact ('We do not know the rules for Old Persian stress, but some rules may be formulated from comparison with other Iranian languages and Indic'): in words of two to four syllables the heavy syllable (long vowel, diphthong, or short vowel followed by more than one consonant) closest to the end of the word, not counting the last syllable, 'probably took the stress' (kā´ra, Višt´āspa, Auramázdā, kāsakáina, mártiya, víspazanā); in words of several short syllables the stress moved toward the beginning of the word (bága, návama) to an unknown limit; whether a closed final syllable could be stressed is unknowable; new penult-stress rules may have developed within the Old Persian period (Middle Persian evidence).
1527.srule: No secondary-stress rule in any source read (Kent 1950 sec. 59(i), Schmitt 2004 sec. 3.4, Skjaervo 2016 p. 18). Kent is silent (accent position and nature unknown); Skjaervo 2016 writes a secondary stress (à) only inside hedged conjectural alternatives for long light-syllable words ('hámaranakara or hamáranakàra (à = secondary stress)'; 'θánuvàniya'), without stating where it falls.

tn.note: Extinct language written in a cuneiform script that marks no accent: enclitics show an accent existed, but whether it was pitch or stress, or kept Indo-Iranian tone, cannot be determined. A second reading (Meillet 1931): Extinct language of the Achaemenid cuneiform inscriptions; the script records neither tone nor accent, and it is impossible to tell whether any trace of the inherited Indo-Iranian tone survived. Checked against the source (tone consistency check, 2026-09-23): evidence impressionistic -> unstated (Kent 1950 sec. 59(i), p. 25).

corr.words: (i) There is no evidence as to the position and nature of the syllabic accent of OP, except that the presence of enclitic words shows that there was an accent.

1527.cfw: Kent 1950, Meillet 1915, Meillet and Benveniste 1931 and Schmitt 2004 all state that the Old Persian cuneiform inscriptions give no evidence for the place or nature of the accent beyond the existence of enclitics, and Skjaervo 2016 offers only a hedged comparative reconstruction (stress on the rightmost non-final heavy syllable) while saying outright that the rules are not known, so the verdict that Old Persian stress is undetermined is the clear consensus.

1528.prule: Dynamic word stress with phonematic (contrastive) value; position irregular in incidence (not fixed to any syllable, explicitly contrasted with Czech/Slovak/Latvian initial and Polish penultimate stress) and mobile within the inflectional paradigm, as in modern Russian; reconstructed for 11th-14th c. Old Russian by projection from the 14th-c. Cudov New Testament, 16th-17th c. accented manuscripts and the modern language.

1529.dq: Todos los cambios que sufrieron las vocales latinas á través del tiempo hasta producir las vocales españolas, se subordinan principalmente al acento de la palabra en que figuran; cada vocal tiene una historia bastante diferente según que está acentuada ó inacentuada ... además del acento principal de una palabra hay uno secundario que hiere las sílabas pares á partir de la tónica
1529.dloc: Cap. II 'Las vocales', opening paragraph immediately before the heading 'Acentuación' (§5), pp. 21-22; secondary accent §24 2], pp. 42-43
1529.prule: Word-accent POSITION inherited unchanged from (Vulgar) Latin into Old and Modern Spanish. Latin placed the accent on the penult if long (by nature or position), else on the antepenult; since Latin quantity is lost in Romance, the Spanish stress position is a lexical inheritance (mostly paroxytone, within the last three syllables), not computable synchronically from syllable count or weight. §6 lists the Vulgar-Latin departures (muta cum liquida penults stressed: intégrum > entero; hiatus shift to the more open vowel: filiólum > hijuelo, OSp. reína/vaína/viúda-type later shifted; prefixed verbs re-accented on the root: renégo > reniego) and learned words with erratic accent.
1529.srule: Secondary accent on the even-numbered syllables counted from the tonic (hu-mì-li-tá-te), stated by Menéndez Pidal for the Latin / Vulgar-Latin base as the mechanism of pretonic syncope (the syllable between the two accents is lost: humildad); not described as a synchronic rhythm of Old Spanish words, post-tonic side not addressed.

1530.prule: Main stress (Hauptton) on the first syllable in simplex words and in nominal compounds (first member); quantity-insensitive, unaffected by derivation ('Abgeleitete Wörter behalten die Betonung des Grundwortes'). Germanic root-initial type.
1530.srule: Secondary stress (Nebenton) is stated and placed (Holthausen 1921 §73): in simplex trisyllabic words it rests on a long medial syllable after a long root syllable (darnungo, mendislo, sorgondi), only exceptionally on a short medial or a position-long final syllable after a long root (gornoda, kesures, waldand); in two-member nominal compounds on the root syllable of the second member (variable in the metre: her-dom, wer-old, en-fald without it; -lik, -skepi nearly unstressed), in three-member compounds on the first syllable of the third member (or-lag-hwila). Weight-conditioned, not alternating.

1531.dq: This should mean that the first and the last syllable of a word had some prominence over the others, or that medial vowels were not stressed. ... default stress on the word's last syllable
1531.dloc: Erdal 2004, A Grammar of Old Turkic, Sec. 2.403 'Syncopation and stress', pp. 97-98
1531.prule: Reconstructed (the scripts do not mark stress): Tekin 2003 par. 147 puts Orkhon Turkic word stress 'generally on the last syllable, apart from certain exceptions', shifting to the last syllable under suffixation (bodún, bodunúm, bodunumín), with a weaker secondary stress on the first syllable of trisyllables and certain suffixes (negative -mA-, imperative, instrumental, equative) leaving the stress on the preceding syllable; Kononov 1980 par. 85 reconstructs the same. Erdal 2004 is more cautious: he says 'we know nothing certain about stress in Old Turkic'; from syncopation of medial vowels he infers only that first and last syllables 'had some prominence', and CONJECTURES ('one would assume') a modern-Turkic-like system: default final-syllable word stress, with initial stress in expressive reduplication and pronominal ka+, pre-stressing negative -mA-, possibly adverbs/instrumental/equative forms.

1532.dq: Late Brythonic had penultimate stress, which became word-final stress as the result of the loss of word-final syllables. In Old Welsh, the stress accent shifted back to the penultimate syllable (Willis); In a polysyllabic word, one syllable is always pronounced with more emphasis than the others ... In Welsh the accent is a stress accent (Morris-Jones sec. 39 i).

tn.quote: Late Brythonic had penultimate stress, which became word-final stress as the result of the loss of word-final syllables. In Old Welsh, the stress accent shifted back to the penultimate syllable, although the pitch accent remained word-final, resulting in the dissociation of stress and pitch accent characteristic of Welsh today. ... In Welsh the accent is a stress accent. ... The first produces musical or pitch accent, the second produces expiratory or stress accent. ... In Keltic, as in Italic and Germanic, the accent became predominantly stress, and has remained so

1535.dloc: Rudin & Shea 2005: Section 2 (Phonology), postprint p. 3 (published vol. 9 pp. 25-29); abstract p. 1. Marsault 2021 thesis: sec. 2.2.3 'Accent and prosody' pp. 98-99 incl. fn. 16; sec. 3.5.1 rule 1 pp. 192-193.
1535.prule: Pitch-based culminative word accent ('downstep pitch accent', Rudin & Shea; 'accent in Umóⁿhoⁿ is based on pitch', Marsault 2021 after Koontz 1988), position lexically determined and unpredictable within a left-edge two-syllable window (Koontz's 'First Two Syllables Constraint'); prefixation shifts the accent leftward to stay in the window; some prefixes (í-, á-, gí-) are inherently accented; a secondary accent appears in words of four or more syllables with unknown placement rules. Rudin & Shea hedge that placement 'may turn out to correlate with vowel length'.
1535.srule: Exists, placement not given: 'When words have four syllables or more, they are regularly written with a second accent in Dorsey’s texts... the rules governing the place of the second accent are unknown. Accents are never placed on contiguous syllables, except in some compounds' (Marsault 2021). Not mentioned in Rudin & Shea 2005, sec. 2 (p. 3).
1535.quote: Vowel length is distinctive in accented syllables (nánande ‘heart’ vs. nánde ‘inside wall’), but this contrast was not recognized by linguists until the 1990s and is still marked only sporadically in written materials. ... A downstep pitch accent occurs on the first or second syllable of the word, and is distinctive: watháthe ‘food’ wáthathe ‘table’, though this may turn out to correlate with vowel length. 1535.exq_: All words are accented on one of the two first syllables16, a feature that Koontz (1988: 3) calls the “First Two Syllables Constraint”. ... [fn. 16] Some exceptions are found, like waiíⁿ ‘robe, tunic’. These exceptions are always words that have a single vowel as one of their syllables.
1535.tone: Source characterises the prosodic system as 'pitch accent' (abstract: 'Notable phonetic features of the language include four series of stops, an unusual dental approximant, and pitch accent'), specifically a 'downstep pitch accent' whose position (syllable 1 vs 2) is lexically distinctive; the word 'stress' appears only once, informally ('imperative enclitics: -ga (male) vs. -a (female), sometimes with stress shift: on’í-ga/on’i-á'). No stress rule separate from the accent is described. Marsault 2021 (sec. 2.2.3): 'According to Koontz (1988), accent in Umóⁿhoⁿ is based on pitch, and every word has “a high-low pitch contour...” The “accent” corresponds to the point of highest pitch in a word. Accent is generally determined lexically, with several minimal pairs distinguished by accentuation... Máxude ‘Baxoje’ vs. maxúde ‘ash, powder’; Wáxe ‘White person’ vs. waxé ‘cache’'; Larson (2009) 'identifies at least four different contours at the syllable level... The syllable contour can be the only signal distinguishing two meanings, which is reminiscent of tone systems'. Sec. 3.5.1: 'according to him [Koontz 1988], the position of the accent on the 1st or 2nd syllable of a root is unpredictable'.

1536.prule: Weight hierarchy, right-oriented: (a) stress a word-final superheavy syllable (CVVC, CVCC, CCVVC) if present; (b) otherwise stress the rightmost NON-FINAL heavy syllable (CVV or CVC; final CVC counts as light by consonant extrametricality); (c) otherwise (all light) stress the leftmost light CV syllable, but never farther left than the antepenult (three-syllable right-edge window). tn.translation: Suárez (1970, 1973) distinguished two tones in Selknam, which would be the same as in Tehuelche: level tone and falling tone ... According to Najlis's (1973) description, in Selknam every syllable has one of two phonologically distinct tones, high (agudo) or low (grave), there being minimal pairs such as those of table 4.34: ... hór 'teeth' hòr 'ravine' ... The main difference is that for Najlis the tones are relevant on every syllable (except those containing the vowels /i/ and /u/), whereas for Suárez ... only syllables with (primary or secondary) stress can bear tone.

Word stress explicitly denied by the dedicated tone study (Farmer & Michael 2013 ms: 'There is no evidence of stress in the language'; 'no obvious metrical basis to tone assignment').

1539.idn: Western dialect of Máíhɨ̃̀kì (Orejón; autonym of the people Máíhùnà), Western Tukanoan, northern Peruvian Amazonia, community of Nueva Vida (F&M 2013); Farmer 2015 describes all three dialects (Western, Eastern, Northern Máíhɨ̃̀kì), fieldwork primarily in Nueva Vida on the Yanayacu River with WM speakers; data: F&M…
1539.tone: Both primaries analyze Maihiki as a contrastive-tone language (H vs L, mora = TBU, root melodies HH/HL/LL; tonal erasure right of the leftmost morpheme in the nominal system; left-aligned HL target by default tone assignment). The thesis (Farmer 2015) does not discuss stress, but the dedicated tone study it defers to (Farmer & Michael 2013 ms) explicitly denies stress: 'Koreguaje is described as tonal, and the existence of a stress system is alluded to by Gralow (1985: 4), but no details are provided. We have found no evidence of stress in Máíhɨ̃̀kì. On the basis of this evidence, then, Máíhɨ̃̀kì appears to be unusual among Tukanoan languages (though not unprecedented, given Barasana) in not exhibiting a stress system, and wholly different from Eastern Tukanoan languages in there being no obvious metrical basis to tone assignment.' Fn. 19: 'Velie (1975: 12-13) and Velie et al. (1976: 11-12) make reference to ‘accent’ in Máíhɨ̃̀kì, but the brief discussions in these works suggest that their ‘accent’ does not correspond to the modern understanding of stress.' Conclusion: 'Máíhɨ̃̀kì does not exhibit a mixed stress-tone system, nor does metrical structure – despite a lack of stress per se – play a role in tonal assignment'. No H-obligatoriness (LL, LLL words allowed) and no culminativity, so not a pitch-accent system either by the authors' account.

morph.stmt: Overwhelmingly suffixing: 'Nouns are marked for the categories of gender, number and case, which are marked by suffixes... 1544.prule: Piggott 1983 (Odawa): (i) every long vowel is stressed; (ii) in a run of short-vowel syllables the even-numbered vowels, counting left to right, are stressed (a short vowel right after a long vowel is not); (iii) the vowel of the word-final syllable is always stressed; (iv) main stress falls on the antepenultimate stressed syllable of a word with three or more stressed syllables, on the penultimate (= first) stressed syllable of a word with two, and on the only stressed syllable otherwise. 1546.prule: Two word-accent classes: 'marked' = stress on the vowel of the LAST syllable, 'neutral' = stress on the PENULTIMATE syllable ('o ninguna en particular'). Penult is the default; final (marked) stress comes from identifiable sources, not free lexical choice: (i) the word-final first-person marker -´y, which attracts stress to the preceding vowel (rimáy 'hablo' vs imperative rímay '¡habla!'; tarpúy 'I sow'); (ii) word-final suffixes that reduce/elide to a single consonant after a short vowel and keep the stress on the now-final vowel (papák < papakta; akšú-k < akšú-kta); (iii) in vowel-final words, a final long vowel ('una vocal final larga requiere la acentuación marcada y una vocal breve la neutra': tukuu [tukú:] 'owl' vs suku [súku] 'hat'). Adelaar & Muysken 2004 state the conditioning as exhaustive -- p.243 (excerpt): 'Pacaraos Quechua presents the particularity of a phonemic stress distinction involving a choice between final and penultimate syllables. Final stress is a characteristic of the first-person marker -y, as in tarpúy 'I sow', and of a number of other suffixes that are subject to elision when in word-final position.'; p.207 (excerpt): '... stress in Pacaraos is either due to the elision of a final syllable, for instance, in akšú-k, from akšú-kta (potato-AC), or to a word-final occurrence of the first-person marker -´y. Otherwise, penultimate stress is...'. The 1982 Léxico frames the resulting surface contrast in consonant-final words as 'función distintiva' ('marcada o neutra según el caso').

A great deal of discussion has taken place, however, on the question of whether, and, if so, when, a stress accent replaced the Vedic accent … Jacobi’s theory would seem to push the transition back before the 4th century B.c., since by that time Pali already possessed its characteristic accent system … If we accept a penultimate stress accent in Pali, with a secondary initial stress … The new stress accent was in Pali apparently not sufficiently felt by the poets

1548.cfw: Three independent standard grammars (Warder 1963, Geiger/Norman 1994, Oberlies 2001) agree that no Pali stress has been transmitted and that quantity, not stress, organises the language, so not determinable from the sources is the clear winner; but Jacobi 1913 positively claims for Pali an intensity accent governed by penult weight, and Geiger's own sec. 4 calls a Sanskritic-type accent 'more likely', so there is a mild, century-old, hedged dissent about the type of system rather than a clean consensus, which is the rubric's 'older source against a modern reference grammar, still a clear winner' case.

1550.prule: Stress weak/levelled; when present it falls on the penultimate syllable, unless the penult contains schwa /ə/, in which case it falls on the final syllable (nera [nəˈra] vs néra [ˈneːra]). 1550.srule: Not mentioned in the primary source (Danerek 2019, sec. 2.2, which treats only disyllables). Per the dedicated stress study Donohue (MS, c. 2004): secondary stress falls on the first syllable of each binary trochaic foot preceding the final, primary-stressed foot, with feet built one per lexical morpheme: quadrisyllables (compounds, reduplications and unanalysable roots alike) are ˌσσˈσσ (ˌoɓoˈtʃava 'pumpkin', basabasa, karapau; ˌvatikəˈba with unstressable epenthetic schwa); bimorphemic trisyllables ˌσːˈσσ (puloga) or ˌσσˈσː (erombu); monomorphemic trisyllables carry no secondary stress (kaˈvala); the proclitic ak- is footed and can bear secondary stress (ˌak-teˈtaʔi), enclitics never.

morph.rootq: Donohue, 'The prosodic structure of Palu'e', sec. 6: 'Clitics form part of the same word, phonologically, as their host, but are not in the domain of stress assignment. This means that a word composed of a root and a clitic will show antepenultimate, rather than penultimate, stress' (loke-gu 'my skin' σ´σσ); sec. 5: 'an input-output rule specifying that the stressed syllable must be a mora in the lexical root: *IO-σ´µ'; sec. 8 on the proclitic ak-: 'being proclitics rather than enclitics, the penultimate stress assignment is not disrupted by presence or absence of the clitic ... the proclitic is parsed into a metrical foot, unlike the enclitics'; sec. 10: 'PARSE (M,ft) each individual…
morph.elicq: Donohue's prosody MS does not state its evidence base; it cites 'phonetically attested stress patterns' and contrasts registers ('This is commonly produced in fast speech as ...', 'in addition to the slow-speech [...]'). Danerek 2019 rests on a documentation corpus plus recorded wordlist readings: 'Data and analysis is drawn from a comprehensive documentation, and specific recordings of three speakers/language variants reading the same wordlist' (abstract); 'each recording took over eight minutes, which is one reason why the words are spoken in isolation and not repeated' (sec. 1.4); fn. 24: 'Stress is, apart from heard, to some extent also visible even in the ELAN media player'.
morph.stmt: Palu'e is described as having no affixes at all and almost no bound morphology: 'there are no affixes in Palu'e' and 'it has little bound morphology, with only some aspectual and adverbial clitics joining the four genitive clitics in the language as enclitics; there are some incipient proclitics, marking case and agreement for 1SG subject' (Donohue 2005b MS fn. 1, sec. 1); 'Palu'e is an extremely isolating SVO-language... The morphology is limited to the four genitive clitics -ku, -mo, -ne, -te' (Danerek 2019 sec. 2.2) -- i.e. what little bound marking exists is overwhelmingly post-root (enclitic), with one optional 1SG proclitic and a fossil prefix te- in a single word.

1551.dq: Pamosu can be classified as a prototypical “stress language”, i.e. a language in which distinctive tone plays no part but which has word level stress. Every word of two syllables or more has contrastive stress on one syllable.
1551.heavy: closed (consonant-final) word-final syllable; 'Words ending in closed syllables generally take stress on the final syllable'. No phonemic vowel length ('There is no phonemic contrast in length').
1551.dflt: open final syllable: initial stress in disyllables (=penult), antepenultimate in words of three or more syllables
1551.prule: Word stress, non-phonemic but with a few derivational minimal pairs. General principles (each hedged 'generally', each with counter-examples): (a) final closed syllable -> final stress, regardless of word class; (b) disyllables with open final syllable -> initial stress; (c) words of 3+ syllables with open final syllable -> antepenultimate stress. Epenthetic /ɔ/ can bear stress under the normal rules.
1551.srule: Secondary stress exists but its placement is not described: Tupper mentions it once, in the pitch-track discussion of [mɛɺindɛnˈdan] 'kind of netbag' (secondary stress on [ɺin], primary on final [ˈdan]); the stress section (§2.3.1) states one contrastive stress per word and gives no rule for secondary stresses.
1551.quote: Pamosu can be classified as a prototypical “stress language”, i.e. a language in which distinctive tone plays no part but which has word level stress. Every word of two syllables or more has contrastive stress on one syllable. Stress is placed in accordance with stress assignment rules which are predictable to speakers ... Given that stress is not phonemically significant, the following description of stress patterns in Pamosu is confined to a few general principles which are apparent from recorded texts. These principles represent generalisations only; every principle is contradicted by coun…

1551.exq_: These principles represent generalisations only; every principle is contradicted by counter-examples, as discussed below. ... There are numerous exceptions to these general principles.
1551.tone: 'distinctive tone plays no part'; stress cues are amplitude and duration, pitch usually higher but word-level pitch declines from the first syllable regardless of stress position.

morph.stmt: Tupper (2012: 56, 58, 290, 292): 'Person and number of subject is expressed by portmanteau suffixes which also indicate tense / mood' while 'the O argument ("object") is expressed by a distinct set of prefixes'; 'The verb has four prefixal slots and three suffixal slots' [(hither)(NEG-)(REM-)(OBJ-) Stem (-DISTR)(-PROG) -Infl, only Stem and suffixal Infl obligatory]; and 'There is little inflection in Pamosu outside the verbal system' -- nouns do not inflect, with case, number and focus carried by postposed free particles/enclitics (case markers 'are independent phonological words rather than affixes', p.521).

1552.dq: These are intonation and its components of pitch level, juncture, and terminal contours (which operate at the level of utterances, phrases, and clauses) and also stress (or vowel length) which sometimes functions to distinguish lexical units.
1552.dloc: sec. 2.2.1 'The Phonemes' (OA ed. pp. 7-8); sec. 2.2.2 'Suprasegmental Features' and 2.3.1 'Stress Shift' (OA ed. pp. 19-20; = orig. 1971 pp. 28-29 per Wikipedia's citation)
1552.prule: Stress (or vowel length -- Forman leaves the phonetic correlate open) is a contrastive/phonemic feature distinguishing lexical items; minimal pairs oppose penultimate vs final stress (ápiq 'lime': apíq 'fire', táu 'person': taú 'feast'). No positional default rule is stated.
1552.srule: Not mentioned in Forman 1971 (secs. 2.1, 2.2.1, 2.2.2, 2.3.1, OA ed. pp. 6-8, 19-21 read: one lexical stress/length feature plus intonation; no secondary or rhythmic stress). Later proposal: Gonzalez 1981 (pp. 16-17, 202) says affixed polysyllabic words may carry more than one accent, the main accent usually on the root and every other accented (affixal/reduplicative) vowel reduced to a secondary value (lalakad 'walking': 2-1); he labels this a non-instrumental proposal and the accent-reduction rules 'not clear at present'.

1553.prule: One stress per phonological word, on the syllable containing the last UNDERLYING (lexical) vowel = surface word-final stress; when the surface-final vowel is the epenthetic [i] (or [ɯ] after /op, ɔp/) that repairs a root-final obstruent/approximant coda, stress is surface-penultimate and that vowel is lengthened (length contrast neutralized). Explicitly weight-insensitive: long vowels and closed syllables never attract stress (HL /pĩn-kõ/ [pĩŋ.ˈkõ]). Compounds/derived words stress the last member (/jɔp-paː/ [jɔp.ˈpaː], /sɔti-pãː/ [sɔ.ˌti.ˈpãː]).

evidence_works.detail: Stress falls on the last lexical (full or long) vowel of the word; when a word ends underlyingly in an oral consonant an epenthetic [i]/[ɯ] is added that never takes stress, so those words surface with penultimate stress and a lengthened stressed vowel ([ˈtɛː.pi] 'fish' from /tɛp/). Long vowels do not pull stress off a following short full vowel ([paː.ˈkɤ] 'shoe'), so the catalog's final-stress rule holds over lexical vowels and the system is only partially quantity-sensitive; the analysis is theoretical (OT with Q-Theory subsegments) over transcribed forms, with no acoustic measurement.
